query: Consider the following context: High-temperature self-lubricating materials with stable tribological performance across a wide temperature range are essential for advanced mechanical systems under extreme conditions. However, balancing mechanical strength and lubrication efficiency remains a key challenge. In that context, which material can be used for high-performance wide-temperature self-lubricating materials, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high‐entropy alloy processed by spark plasma sintering of inert gas atomized powders can serve as a high-performance wide-temperature self-lubricating material because its multiphase microstructure promotes the in situ formation of a protective oxide (spinel) film at elevated temperatures, thereby balancing mechanical strength with reduced friction and wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A dense, SPS-processed AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy with a multiphase (primarily dual BCC phases with minor tetragonal σ-phase) microstructure and high hardness (~750 HV) produced by inert gas atomization.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to reciprocating wear testing over a wide temperature range (from room temperature up to 900 °C) under atmospheric conditions.
generation.conditions: Reciprocating wear tests using defined parameters (e.g., 26 N force, 40 Hz frequency, 0.5 mm amplitude, 900 s duration) in air with passive cooling to simulate service conditions across a broad temperature range.
generation.structural_mediator: The thermally activated formation of a protective spinel oxide phase (with a structure analogous to MgAl2O4) on the worn surface.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, tribo-oxidation leads to the development of a continuous, low-shear oxide film that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact while the inherent high-strength microstructure sustains mechanical load. This oxide film effectively provides self-lubrication by lowering friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: At high temperatures (near 900 °C), the alloy is expected to exhibit a lower coefficient of friction (approaching ~0.85) and reduced wear depth compared to room temperature conditions, while maintaining its high hardness and strength, thus achieving stable tribological performance across the testing range.
generation.baseline: Under room temperature wear conditions, the alloy shows higher friction and wear depth due to the absence of a fully developed protective oxide layer.
generation.boundary: The beneficial self-lubricating behavior is expected to hold up to approximately 900 °C under ambient atmospheric conditions; performance may degrade if temperatures significantly exceed this range or if the environmental atmosphere alters oxide stability.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in friction coefficient and wear depth is uncertain due to potential variability in oxide layer formation kinetics and testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA specimens via spark plasma sintering and perform reciprocating wear tests at a series of temperatures (e.g., RT, 500 °C, 650 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C). Concurrently, use XRD and SEM/TEM to analyze the worn surfaces for the presence and continuity of the oxide (spinel) film.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) at each test temperature
Phase identification (via XRD) of oxide formation on the wear tracks
Microstructural imaging (SEM/TEM) to assess the protective film thickness and continuity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the protective oxide film does not form or if there is no significant reduction in COF and wear depth at elevated temperatures compared to room temperature, the hypothesis that the in situ formed oxide provides self-lubrication and improved tribological performance will be falsified.

Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
